verdict.reasoning: The doctor states the patient is having lip swelling after eating, and the patient clarifies it was prawn soup; the doctor later says, “it sounds like you could be going into what we say, anaphylactic reaction,” showing concern for anaphylaxis.
Patient says she went with friends to a place to eat and “ordered a prawn soup… just after work. So maybe like around seven,” which is a dining setting at approximately 7:00 pm involving prawns.

When asked, “how long did it take to develop the swelling?” the patient answers, “must have been like, I don’t know, half an hour maybe,” and later adds, “there is like a swelling on my upper lip and it’s kind of getting bigger. It feels like it’s getting worse.”

The doctor asks about throat swelling and chest tightness; patient replies, “I feel like I can’t breathe that well,” and “Chest just generally feels a little difficult,” indicating throat/breathing and chest symptoms.
Patient opens with, “I feel a little weird today, to be honest,” indicating she currently feels unwell.

Patient recalls a year-ago episode: “I woke up the next morning quite swollen up and had also like… felt really bad and quite difficult breathing,” but there is no mention that it required medical care at that time.

The transcript does not say the mother recalls the prior reaction a year ago; instead, the patient says, “I think I remember my mom told me about it,” regarding an injection in childhood, which was not explicitly tied to the episode a year ago.

Doctor asks if she ever had to use an injection for peanut allergy; she replies only that her mom told her about one when she was small. There is no report of her self-administering epinephrine, supporting the statement that there is no history of self-administered epinephrine use.
Patient says, “I generally have asthma… I generally have asthma,” confirming a history of asthma.
Patient states, “I take… what’s it called? Salbutamol inhalus… Yeah. So I do take that regularly,” confirming regular salbutamol inhaler use.
Doctor asks about antihistamines; patient answers, “Sometimes, but I don’t know which ones,” indicating intermittent use with unknown specific agent.
When asked if she has any antihistamines with her, she replies, “No, I don’t think I have,” indicating she does not currently have any.
Patient says, “So I have a peanut allergy as well. Yeah, like always had it?” confirming peanut allergy.
Doctor asks if anyone is with her; patient says, “Alone at the moment.” Later she says, “Somebody just came… Yes, Mom,” showing she was initially alone and her mother then arrived.

Exposure to prawns is described; patient has lip swelling and breathing/chest symptoms; doctor says, “it sounds like you could be going into… anaphylactic reaction,” supporting suspected anaphylaxis to prawns with those symptoms.

The patient has “a peanut allergy,” “I generally have asthma,” and describes a prior episode with “quite swollen up and… quite difficult breathing” after food, consistent with a prior severe food-related reaction.

Doctor indicates concern and plans escalation: “we need to call an ambulance,” “you might need an injection,” and instructs, “So straight away, take the antihistamines in the meantime,” indicating ambulance/escalation, interim antihistamine, and potential epinephrine.

Doctor says, “we need to call an ambulance… I’ll send them right to you,” and later instructs mom to “call the 999… they need to come straight away,” and to have “that person’s with you till the ambulance comes,” indicating immediate EMS transport with caregiver present.
Doctor asks if anyone has antihistamines and then says, “So straight away, take the antihistamines in the meantime,” directing their use once available under his guidance.
There is no explicit instruction in the transcript about monitoring progression of symptoms or avoiding further allergen exposure, so these elements are not documented.

Doctor explains the situation “sounds like… an anaphylactic reaction” and that “you might need an injection. Like what your mom told you as you were a young child,” and states she needs to go to hospital, implying preparation for epinephrine and ED evaluation by EMS.

Doctor says, “Come out from the hospital. Do give us a ring back. We might need to sort you out with your injections and things like that,” indicating follow-up with the general practice/doctor after ED care.

Patient describes “a swelling on my upper lip,” “I feel like I can’t breathe that well,” and “Chest just generally feels a little difficult,” consistent with lip swelling, dyspnea, and chest tightness; throat fullness is implied by the breathing difficulty in context of the doctor’s question about throat closing.
She reports symptom onset timing: “must have been like, I don’t know, half an hour maybe,” after eating the prawn soup at about 7 pm.
There is no documentation of vital signs or a formal physical examination in the transcript; only symptom history is discussed.
